opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, CDC is one of those things that sounds simple in principle but gets surprisingly tricky in practice. The basic idea is great: instead of periodically dumping the whole database, you tap into the transaction log, the stream of inserts, updates, and deletes, and replay it into your analytics system so you have an up-to-date copy of the operational state. And it's become the default way a lot of companies feed their lakehouse, because full snapshots just don't scale once your tables get large.

But reconstructing state correctly is harder than people expect. First, ordering and exactly-once semantics really matter. If you apply an update before the insert, or replay a batch twice after a failure, your copy quietly drifts from the source. Second, you have to handle schema changes. Someone adds a column or changes a type in Postgres, and the pipeline has to evolve the downstream table without breaking. Third, there's the initial snapshot plus the ongoing stream. Stitching those together consistently, so you don't miss or double-count changes during the handoff, is a classic source of bugs.

Then there's the storage side. Analytics formats like Parquet were designed for big immutable files, not lots of small row-level updates. That's a big part of why we built things like MERGE support, deletion vectors, and change data feed into Delta Lake. You want to apply a high volume of upserts efficiently, and then let downstream consumers read just what changed instead of rescanning everything.

So my view is that CDC is the right primitive. It's fundamentally the log, and the log is the source of truth. But historically every team ended up building their own fragile pipeline around it. The direction I'm excited about is making it declarative: you say "keep this table in sync with that source," and the system handles ordering, retries, schema evolution, and compaction for you. Ideally the operational database and the analytics side get close enough that you barely think about CDC as a separate pipeline at all. It's just how data flows.

r001.rationale: The response describes CDC pipeline bugs and fragility, but does not identify failures as a source of late-night operational work for data engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so CDC is one of those things that sounds simple and turns out to be surprisingly subtle. The basic idea is: your operational database already has a log of every change — inserts, updates, deletes — and instead of periodically dumping the whole table, you tail that log and replay it somewhere else. In principle that gives you a near-real-time replica of the database state in your analytics system without hammering the production database with big scans.

The reason it's hard is that a stream of changes is not the same thing as a table. To reconstruct state, you have to apply those changes in order, handle updates and deletes correctly, deal with schema changes, and you have to do it in a way that's idempotent, because the pipeline will fail and restart and you'll see duplicates. If you get any of that wrong, the copy quietly drifts from the source, and people lose trust in the analytics system very quickly.

That's actually one of the things that motivated a lot of the work on Delta Lake. If your analytics storage layer only supports appending files, CDC is really painful — you end up with these giant append-only change logs that you have to compact and dedupe with custom jobs, and everyone writes their own slightly broken version of that. Once you have ACID transactions and a MERGE operation on the lake, applying a CDC feed becomes a pretty standard pattern: you land the changes, you merge them into the target table in batches, and you get a consistent snapshot that query engines can read. Time travel also helps, because you can go back and audit what the table looked like at a given point.

The other thing I'd say is that latency expectations matter a lot. Most people say they want real-time, but for the vast majority of analytics use cases, a few minutes is fine, and doing CDC in micro-batches is much cheaper and easier to reason about than true record-at-a-time streaming. So I'd view CDC less as a streaming problem and more as a correctness problem: how do you keep a faithful, queryable copy of a changing system, with clean semantics, that you can rebuild if something goes wrong. The storage layer with transactions is what makes that tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says pipelines can fail and restart, causing duplicate changes and possible drift, but it does not identify those failures as a source of late-night operational work for data engineers.

astra-6.text:
I think CDC is a very useful building block, but it’s not quite the same thing as having a replica of the database. You’re getting a stream of changes, and then your analytics system has to interpret those changes correctly to reconstruct the state.

Typically, you start with a snapshot and apply the changes after that. The tricky part is making sure there’s no gap between the snapshot and the change stream, and handling things like ordering, retries, and deletes. If you replay an event, you don’t want to apply an update twice. And if a transaction changes multiple records, you have to decide whether the analytics system needs to expose those changes atomically.

So it’s a good way to keep an analytics system up to date without repeatedly scanning the source database. But the correctness comes from the whole pipeline—the snapshot, the change capture, and how you apply the changes—not just from having a log of events.

r001.rationale: The response discusses CDC correctness risks such as gaps, ordering, retries, and deletes, but does not say that pipeline failures cause late-night operational work for data engineers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think CDC is a very useful building block, but there’s a difference between getting a stream of changes and reconstructing the database’s state correctly. You need a consistent starting snapshot, and then you need to apply the changes without gaps, with the right ordering and handling of updates and deletes. If something fails and you replay part of that stream, you also need to avoid applying a change twice.

And then there’s the question of consistency across tables. If a transaction updates two tables, you probably don’t want your analytics query to see one update but not the other. So CDC can absolutely support this, but there’s a fair amount of machinery between capturing the changes and giving users a reliable, queryable view of the database.

r001.rationale: The response says failures require replay handling, but does not identify CDC pipeline failures as causing late-night operational work for data engineers.
